title: Paul VI (1963–1978)
hook: the pope who boarded planes to Jerusalem, India and New York, and told the United Nations no more war

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vatican II lived: the day the priest turned around. Your line was the council in the pews. What did you hear from someone who remembers? Today, the pope who carried that council to its end. Day nine hundred nineteen.

A thin man in white walks to a podium in New York. In front of him sit the representatives of the world's nations, in the hall of the United Nations General Assembly. He is the bishop of Rome, a long way from Rome. He came by plane. He has no army and no vote in this hall. He tells them he has nothing to ask for himself. Then, speaking in French, he says the words this day is built on. No more war. War never again. His name was Giovanni Battista Montini. As pope he was called Paul the Sixth.
screen: `A MAN IN WHITE IN NEW YORK.` → `NO ARMY, NOTHING TO ASK.` → `NO MORE WAR.`

segments.voice: Paul the Sixth came right after Good Pope John, and he is easy to overlook. Here are four ways in. First, the finisher. John called the council; Paul was elected between its sessions, with much of its work still ahead, and he brought it to its close and began putting it into practice. The Mass in local languages you remembered yesterday came in under him. Second, the traveler. He took the name of Paul, the apostle who crossed the sea again and again, and he got on airplanes. He went to Jerusalem and embraced the Orthodox patriarch Athenagoras there. He went to India. He went to New York. Third, the speech. At the United Nations he spoke of himself as an expert in humanity, a man with long experience of human beings, and he begged the nations: no more war, war never again. He told them that if they wanted to be brothers, they should let the weapons fall from their hands. Catholics hear in this the old promise in Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they be exercised any more to war." Fourth, the cost. Paul's years were not calm. Some of his teaching, especially his letter on marriage and birth control, was hard for some Catholics to accept, and it is still argued over. The Church has since named him a saint. What stays is a man without an army, standing in a hall of flags, asking the nations to put the weapons down.
screen: `THE POPE WHO FINISHED THE COUNCIL.` · `THE TRAVELER: JERUSALEM, INDIA, NEW YORK.` · `AT THE UN: NO MORE WAR.` · `A HARD PAPACY, A SAINT.` · then, large: `NATION SHALL NOT LIFT UP SWORD AGAINST NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the United Nations in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring up that hall, the rows of desks, the name of each country on a card. Then the people behind the cards: diplomats who haven't slept, translators in their booths, peacekeepers far from home, staff who feed refugees. Pick one of them and stay with that person for a while. If you pray, you can pray for them, perhaps with Isaiah's line about swords. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them steady hands. The bell holds the time.
Paul the Sixth. The pope who finished the council, traveled by plane, and told the nations at the UN: no more war.
Your line: no more war. Today, when a news story about a war crosses your screen, stop on it for one breath instead of scrolling past, and say the line. Day nine hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Paul VI, and the Holy See keeps a permanent observer at the United Nations, where later popes have also addressed the General Assembly.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'first pope to fly around the world' is a superlative not supported by a cited text; replaced with the places he flew to. No dates spoken.
UN address: confirm 'expert in humanity', 'nothing to ask for himself', 'jamais plus la guerre, jamais plus la guerre' and 'let the weapons fall from your hands' (paraphrased).
Meeting with Athenagoras in Jerusalem and the visit to India (Bombay): confirm.
Humanae Vitae described as 'hard for many to accept and still argued over among Catholics': this is a 'many' claim; Keeper to approve or soften.
howItsDone says popes since Paul VI have addressed the General Assembly; confirm or cut.
Isaiah 2:4 Douay-Rheims wording ('exercised any more to war'): confirm exactly.
Editor pass: hook line about 'no army... and he says so' untangled; unsourced 'he carried that weight quietly' cut.

Second editor pass: 'standing between Good Pope John and John Paul the Second' was wrong (John Paul I came between); now 'came right after Good Pope John'. Closing line 'the one thing none of them could give him: peace' replaced with a concrete image of the UN hall and his plea to put weapons down.

Audit pass: 'elected while it was still meeting' was wrong (he was elected in the recess between the first and second sessions); now 'between its sessions'. Trapdoor's first two floors rewritten because 'a pope only speaks to Catholics' repeated day 917's trapdoor almost word for word.
